text: The sum of all natural numbers 1 + 2 + 3 + ... = -1/12 in Ramanujan summation. It appears in string theory.
A pizza that has radius 'z' and height 'a' has volume Pi × z × z × a.
There are exactly as many even numbers as there are natural numbers. Infinity is strange.
Euler's identity e^(iπ) + 1 = 0 connects five fundamental constants in one equation.
If you shuffle a deck of cards properly, the resulting order has almost certainly never existed before in human history.
"Mathematics is the queen of the sciences and number theory is the queen of mathematics." (Carl Friedrich Gauss, as reported in Sartorius von Waltershausen, Gauss zum Gedächtniss, 1856)
A Möbius strip has only one side. Cut it down the middle and you get one longer strip, not two.
0.999... = 1 exactly. Not approximately. They are the same number.
The word 'algebra' comes from the Arabic 'al-jabr', meaning 'reunion of broken parts'.
There are more real numbers between 0 and 1 than there are natural numbers in total.
"Pure mathematics is, in its way, the poetry of logical ideas." (Albert Einstein, letter to The New York Times on Emmy Noether, 1935)
The Banach-Tarski paradox: using the axiom of choice, a solid ball can be cut into 5 pieces and reassembled into two balls the same size as the original.
Galois, a founder of group theory, was fatally wounded in a duel at age 20. The night before, he wrote a long letter to a friend summarizing his mathematical ideas.
A random walk on a 2D grid will return to its starting point with probability 1. In 3D, the probability is only about 34%.
"God made the integers, all the rest is the work of man." (Leopold Kronecker, 1886 lecture, as reported by Heinrich Weber, 1893)
The number 1729 is the smallest number expressible as the sum of two positive cubes in two different ways: 1³+12³ and 9³+10³.
Every even number greater than 2 appears to be the sum of two primes; computers have checked it up to 4 × 10^18. Nobody has proven it (Goldbach's conjecture).
Sunflower heads and pinecones often show spiral counts that are consecutive Fibonacci numbers, such as 34 and 55. Popular claims that galaxy arms follow the same pattern are not supported.
There are infinitely many primes. Euclid proved this around 300 BC and the proof still fits in a paragraph.
"In mathematics the art of proposing a question must be held of higher value than solving it." (Georg Cantor, doctoral thesis, 1867)
The four color theorem (any flat map can be colored with 4 colors so that neighboring regions always differ) was the first major theorem proved with a computer, in 1976.
If you could fold a piece of paper 42 times, it would reach the Moon. Exponential growth is wild.
Gödel showed in 1931 that any consistent formal system strong enough to express basic arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove.
The digits of π never repeat and never end. After trillions of digits computed, no pattern has been found.

"The measure of our success is whether what we do enables people to understand and think more clearly and effectively about mathematics." (William Thurston, "On Proof and Progress in Mathematics", 1994)
A group of 23 people has a 50% chance that two share a birthday. With 70 people, it's 99.9%.
Emmy Noether's theorem links every continuous symmetry in physics to a conservation law. Symmetry of time → conservation of energy.
The classification of finite simple groups is one of the longest proofs in mathematics: tens of thousands of pages in several hundred papers by about 100 authors.
Ramanujan, self-taught in India, sent letters to Hardy with results so remarkable they changed number theory forever.
"Do not worry about your difficulties in Mathematics. I can assure you mine are still greater." (Albert Einstein, letter to Barbara Lee Wilson, 1943)
A Klein bottle is a closed surface with no inside or outside. To exist without passing through itself, it needs at least four dimensions.
The Collatz conjecture is simple to state (if even, halve it; if odd, triple and add 1) but nobody can prove it always reaches 1.
2 is the only even prime number, making it the oddest prime.
Euler was so prolific that his unpublished papers kept appearing in print until about 1830, nearly 50 years after his death.
"The essence of mathematics lies entirely in its freedom." (Georg Cantor, Grundlagen einer allgemeinen Mannigfaltigkeitslehre, 1883)
The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ... diverges to infinity, but incredibly slowly. You need ~10^43 terms to reach 100.
Topology considers a coffee mug and a donut to be the same shape: both have exactly one hole.
The Mandelbrot set is generated by the simple formula z → z² + c, yet contains infinite complexity at every zoom level.
There are problems that are provably unsolvable: not just hard, but literally impossible for any algorithm (the Halting Problem).
"Mathematics, rightly viewed, possesses not only truth, but supreme beauty." (Bertrand Russell, "The Study of Mathematics", 1907)
The digits 142857 × {1,2,3,4,5,6} produce cyclic permutations of themselves. It's called a cyclic number.
Cantor's work on infinity drew fierce attacks, notably from Kronecker, and he suffered repeated bouts of depression. Today his set theory is foundational.
P vs NP (whether problems that are easy to verify are also easy to solve) has a $1 million bounty.

The golden ratio φ = (1+√5)/2 ≈ 1.618 is the 'most irrational' number: its continued fraction is all 1s, so in a precise sense it is the hardest number to approximate by fractions. Its role in famous art is mostly myth.
Andrew Wiles proved Fermat's Last Theorem in 1995 after working on it secretly for 7 years.
"They must be true because, if they were not true, no one would have had the imagination to invent them." (G. H. Hardy, on Ramanujan's formulas, Ramanujan: Twelve Lectures, 1940)
The probability of a monkey randomly typing Shakespeare is not zero, just astronomically small.
Zero was independently invented in Mesopotamia, India, and Mesoamerica. It took Europe centuries to accept it.
e^(iτ) = 1 where τ = 2π. Some mathematicians argue τ is more natural than π.
"Ask your own questions, look for your own examples, discover your own proofs." (Paul Halmos, on reading mathematics, I Want to Be a Mathematician, 1985)
A sphere can be turned inside out without cutting, tearing or creasing it, as long as it may pass through itself. This is Smale's paradox.
The Riemann Hypothesis, if proven, would reveal the deep pattern behind prime numbers. $1 million bounty.
In base 12, multiplication tables are simpler because 12 has more factors than 10.
Hypatia of Alexandria (died 415 AD) was one of the first recorded female mathematicians and a renowned philosopher.
There are exactly 5 Platonic solids (tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron). This has been proven since antiquity.
"Music is a hidden arithmetic exercise of the soul, which does not know that it is counting." (Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, letter to Christian Goldbach, 1712)
The Monty Hall problem: switching doors gives you a 2/3 chance of winning, not 1/2. Even mathematicians got this wrong at first.
Many fractals have fractional dimensions. The Koch snowflake has dimension log(4)/log(3) ≈ 1.26.
Hilbert's Hotel: a hotel with infinitely many rooms can always accommodate more guests, even infinitely many.

"The scientist does not study nature because it is useful to do so. He studies it because he takes pleasure in it, and he takes pleasure in it because it is beautiful." (Henri Poincaré, Science and Method, 1908)
Gabriel's Horn has finite volume but infinite surface area. You can fill it with paint but never paint its surface.
In 1843 Ada Lovelace published a method for Babbage's Analytical Engine to compute Bernoulli numbers, often called the first computer program.
The sum of interior angles of a triangle on a sphere is always MORE than 180°. Geometry depends on curvature.
There are 177,147 ways to tie a necktie, according to a mathematical analysis of knot sequences.
"If people do not believe that mathematics is simple, it is only because they do not realize how complicated life is." (John von Neumann, 1947, as recalled by Franz Alt, 1972)
Nash equilibrium, the idea behind John Nash's 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics, shows how rational players can settle on stable outcomes that are worse for everyone.
Euler discovered that V - E + F = 2 for any convex polyhedron. Vertices minus edges plus faces always equals 2.
The word 'calculus' comes from the Latin for 'small pebble': Romans used pebbles for counting.
A regular 17-gon can be constructed with compass and straightedge; Gauss proved this in 1796, as a teenager. A popular story says he wanted one carved on his tombstone.
"No one has yet discovered any warlike purpose to be served by the theory of numbers or relativity." (G. H. Hardy, A Mathematician's Apology, 1940) Number theory now underpins RSA encryption.
Benford's Law: in many real-world datasets, the leading digit is 1 about 30% of the time, not 11% as you'd expect.
The Brouwer fixed-point theorem: stir an idealized cup of coffee smoothly, without splashing, and at least one point of the liquid ends up exactly where it started.
Turing proved that the Halting Problem is undecidable in 1936, before electronic computers even existed.
i^i (where i = √-1) is a real number: its principal value is e^(-π/2), approximately 0.2079.
"We must know. We shall know." (David Hilbert, retirement address, Königsberg, 1930). The words are carved on his tombstone in Göttingen.
The number of possible chess games exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe.
Fermat scribbled 'I have a truly marvelous proof' in a margin. It took 358 years for anyone to find one.
The hairy ball theorem: you can't comb a hairy sphere flat without creating a cowlick. At any moment, the horizontal wind must be zero somewhere on Earth.
Every positive integer is the sum of at most 4 perfect squares. Lagrange proved this in 1770.
"Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them." (Alfred North Whitehead, An Introduction to Mathematics, 1911)
If you pick a number uniformly at random between 0 and 1, the probability that it is rational is exactly 0, even though rationals are everywhere.
The derivative of e^x is e^x. It's the only function (up to scaling) that is its own derivative.
Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier when Syracuse fell around 212 BC. His famous last words, 'Do not disturb my circles,' appear in no ancient source.
ln(2) = 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - 1/4 + ... This beautiful series converges to the natural log of 2.
Drop a needle onto a floor ruled with parallel lines one needle-length apart: it crosses a line with probability 2/π. This is Buffon's needle, a way to estimate π by chance.
The twin prime conjecture (that infinitely many primes differ by 2) remains unproven, though since 2014 it is known that infinitely many pairs of primes differ by at most 246.
"Life is good for only two things: doing mathematics and teaching it." (Siméon Poisson, as reported by François Arago, 1854)
Gödel starved himself to death, fearing poisoning. Only his wife could convince him to eat; when she was hospitalized, he stopped.
